positions.thesis: Raised from 18% on a print that post-dates my fill and validates the thesis. Q2 on 8/4 delivered adjusted $0.77 against $0.68 consensus, a fifth consecutive beat, and management raised the low end of the revenue outlook - the pattern I sized into. At $26.76 it is still 9.64x forward against a 19x industry, yields 6.43%, and sits ~7% below the $28.64 consensus target and well under its $28.75 peak. The pipeline news is additive rather than load-bearing: positive Phase 3 LITFULO data in vitiligo, FDA priority review on a prostate-cancer combination, EU authorisation of the updated COVID formula. Critically, this is the one holding with no AI-capex duration and no economic cyclicality, and its 6.4% yield gets MORE attractive as the long end falls on a negative payroll print - the same repricing that hurts my cyclical sleeve helps this one. Keeping the -18% stop wide so a valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by a single bad tape day.

Raised from 12% because the precise reason I gave for keeping it small has reversed. I wrote that a 6% bond-proxy yield was a thin spread against a 5.28% 30-year with a September hike being priced; payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions, hike odds dropped 58% to 42%, the 10-year fell 7bp to 4.65% and the 30-year to 5.20%. Short-duration contracted cash flows re-rate on a dovish repricing. The fundamentals are unchanged and good: 9.28x forward, a 6.01% dividend covered by free cash flow, beta 0.24, buyback target raised to $4.5bn, raised 2026 guidance, and the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent instead of costing it multiple. The reason this is 15% and not 20% is a genuine new negative: reporting that SpaceX believes it can build wireless capability without massive network investment pressured the group, and direct-to-cell is a real long-run terminal-value question I cannot dismiss.

Trimmed from 15%. Part of my case was explicitly two-thirds odds of a September hike as a direct NIM tailwind; those odds are now 42%, and a labour market printing negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward credit-cost signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered. Partially offsetting, a dovish front-end repricing steepens the curve, which is the larger NIM driver, so this is a trim and not an exit. What still holds is the valuation: at $135.00 it is 11.56x forward, the cheapest large-cap US bank, with Q2 net income of $5.8bn on $24.77bn revenue, ROTCE at 13%, and a $154.50 consensus implying ~14% upside. And I keep my own correction on the record - at $100.89 TBVPS this is ~1.34x tangible, not the sub-book story I once claimed, so there is no buyback-accretion kicker here. The $127 no-news flush I bought has fully mean-reverted, so the specific dislocation is harvested; what is left is an ordinary cheap bank, worth 13% and not 15%. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate will keep the group volatile in both directions.

Cut from 16% - I am unwinding the macro add, not the value holding. I raised this to 16% eight days ago explicitly citing Brent at $88-90, up 20% on the month, with Iran attacking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent is now $83.55 after a decline of more than 7% on the week on reporting of a potential Iran-Oman agreement to restore Hormuz shipping, and a negative payroll print adds demand-side risk. The premium I paid up for is deflating, and I should not keep an oversized position justified by a catalyst that is reversing. The company leg is genuinely excellent and is why I keep a real 11%: record Q2 with $12.1bn net income against $2.5bn a year ago, production up 20% on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement, 12.21x forward, a 3.82% yield, beta 0.49 and a $216.96 consensus 16% above spot. Brent at $83.55 is still up 25% year over year, so this remains a sub-market-multiple FCF payer and the book's inflation hedge - just at a size set by the business rather than by a headline.

Held flat, and deliberately not cut alongside CVX because the crude move helps this line rather than hurting it. A refiner buys crude and sells product: Brent falling more than 7% while refining margins are described as at extreme levels is the favourable configuration, feedstock cheapening before cracks follow it down. Q2 confirmed the operating leverage - $3.7bn net income, adjusted $12.54 against $10.22 consensus, refining operating income $4.5bn against $1.3bn a year ago, renewable diesel swinging to $717m of operating income, $2.6bn returned at a 59% payout. But that print was already in my 7/31-close entry and is not a reason to add, and at $298.31 against a $320.24 high with the market cap already doubled, consensus sees only 3.85% upside. So it earns its 9% at 7.82x forward and no more. The +20% take-profit harvests a distillate-crack blowout without my having to time the exit, and the -18% stop covers the reversal case where crude stops falling and cracks compress.

Raised from 5% on the same duration logic that lifts VZ, plus a correction to my own numbers. I had been carrying this at 13.1x forward; it is actually 11.86x, with a 6.20% yield and beta 0.50, and Q2 showed adjusted EPS and OCI growth on smokables plus an expanding smoke-free portfolio with FY26 guidance narrowed to $5.61-5.72. I sized this at only 5% explicitly because a ~6% bond proxy was the wrong duration against a 5.28% 30-year with a hike priced; with the 30-year at 5.20%, hike odds at 42% and payrolls outright negative, near-zero-beta contracted carry is worth more, not less. It stays capped at 7% for the reason I gave before and which has not changed: at $68.35 against a $77.06 high and a $70.64 consensus target, the deep-value discount here is largely closed, so this is ballast and carry rather than a discount trade.

Trimmed 6% to 5% and kept deliberately vestigial. The mandate requires a small short in the most stretched growth cohort, and at a 44.71x P/E with the fund 21.7% NVIDIA, SMH is still honestly that cohort - ARKK is flat over twelve months and shorting it would not be shorting anything stretched. But I have now lost the argument twice over. First the catalyst: hyperscaler capex doubt inverted into ~$650bn of confirmed 2026 spend with semis as the direct recipients. Now the discount rate: a negative payroll print and hike odds falling to 42% lower the discount rate on exactly the long-duration cash flows I am short. And the tape is hostile in a measurable way - SMH +1.96% on 8/7 with SOXL +5.99% the same session, and five shorts in this and the gold-miner complex stopped out on that single day. That is a live squeeze and I am on the wrong side of it, so I size for survival, not for a view: 5% of NAV with a -22% stop risks about 1.1% of the book, and 3% borrow with no funding cost on shorts makes the carry negligible. It stays as insurance against a broad de-rating that would hit my long book, not as a bet that semis fall.

positions.thesis: Core anchor, raised from 33% to 36%. Head-to-head against its two rivals this week SCHD wins on every axis that matters to this mandate: +31.73% trailing 1yr total return versus DGRO's +25.21% and NOBL's +16.32%, a 3.09% yield versus 1.86% and 1.99%, and a 0.06% fee versus 0.08% and 0.35%. It now holds $105.7B across 103 quality-screened dividend growers. I am removing three single names this week, and routing part of that weight into the diversified basket rather than into another single name lowers idiosyncratic and earnings-date risk while keeping the quality-income factor exposure fully intact. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket.

Upsized from 8% to 11% and now my largest single name. Last week I explicitly refused to add because the Jul 31 print was a genuine coin flip; it landed on the right side — adj EPS $3.65 versus $3.61 consensus, management calling it 'another excellent quarter,' FY26 revenue guidance RAISED to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, Skyrizi momentum in immunology, EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata and FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. Yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 Buy consensus, +11.1%. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.81% yield where the event risk is banked and the price is lower than before the event is the single best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. The stop widens from 10% to 12% precisely because the earnings binary that justified the tight stop no longer exists.

Upsized from 8% to 9% and now the larger of my two energy legs. A 38-year raiser yielding 3.82% — the highest yield in the entire book — at 12.21x forward earnings, with quarterly net income of $12.1B against $2.5B a year ago and a $216.96 consensus implying 16.3% upside. Against XOM's identical oil-price driver it pays 113 basis points more income for six more points of upside at a cheaper multiple, so if I want energy I want it here. Held to single digits rather than pushed harder because the earnings are levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium that can deflate overnight, it fell 1.41% on a day the S&P rose 0.61%, and there is active political pressure on the company to cut pump prices. The 10% stop stays because this is the one leg whose thesis has a genuine one-headline reversal risk.

Trimmed from 13% to 9%. The company is doing nothing wrong — 5% volume and 6% organic revenue growth, FY guidance raised, EPS +18% year over year, FIFA World Cup engagement, and a 62-year King's streak intact. What changed is the price: at $87.05 against a $94.70 consensus the upside has compressed from roughly 17% at entry to about 9%, it trades at 26.2x for a 2.44% yield, and it sits close to its $90.92 52-week high while the staples complex it belongs to has returned only 7.18% over a year. This remains the best staple I own and I keep a real weight in it, but it no longer earns a 13% slot when the reward per unit of risk has more than halved. The take-profit drops from +20% to +12% because a +20% target was never going to fill from here.

New position, funded by the P&G exit. A 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat yielding 3.30% — the richest yield available among healthcare aristocrats — with a 0.57 beta, FY26 revenue up 8.43% to $36.36B, and a Buy consensus at $98.44 against $87.16, or 12.9% upside. It trades in the bottom third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, so I am buying defensive quality on sale rather than chasing. Pipeline is moving: expanded CE Mark for the Affera mapping and ablation system into ventricular arrhythmias, plus closed acquisitions of SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular. Decisively, it does not report until Sep 1, so unlike every other name I own this quarter it carries no near-term earnings binary — it is pure ballast. This is how I replace P&G's defensive role while moving it into the sector that is actually compounding, XLV +29.17% against XLP +7.18%.

Trimmed from 9% to 7%. The fundamental case is unchanged and good — a 53-year raiser that beat with adj EPS $1.31 and raised FY EPS guidance, with FDA clearance to commercialize the SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test opening a new diagnostics market, and the DOJ criminal probe into the formula facility now closed, which removes a legal overhang. I trim rather than hold flat for two specific reasons: at 34.9x trailing the consensus offers only 9.84% upside to $118.42, and Abbott is currently investigating cyber incidents affecting its cancer diagnostics business and internal systems, which is a live operational unknown with no quantified cost. I also already own it indirectly at 4.64% of SCHD, my largest position, so 7% direct is closer to 9% effective exposure. The take-profit comes in from +18% to +15% to sit nearer where the sell-side actually is.

Trimmed from 7% to 6% and deliberately kept behind CVX. The quarter was excellent in absolute terms — $14.5B of earnings on $23.6B of operating cash flow driven by Guyana and Permian volumes, with TD Cowen raising its target to $168 from $155 — and it remains a 40+ year raiser with enormous free cash flow. But it yields 2.69% against Chevron's 3.82% and offers roughly 10% upside against Chevron's 16.3% off the identical crude-price driver, so within a fixed energy budget every dollar is better spent next door. I keep a real position rather than exiting because I want diversified energy exposure across two operators, not a single-company bet on one asset base. Total energy sits at 15%, unchanged in size but improved in mix.

Held flat at 5%. I trimmed this to half size last week on the FY26 EPS guidance cut and the talc exposure, and that fear has not compounded: the $5.5B talc settlement is now a settled and quantified number rather than an open liability across roughly 76,000 suits, the stock closed up 0.88% at $259.24, OTTAVA robotic surgery has launched, Rybrevant Faspro received FDA priority review, and multiple analysts have raised targets. I do not add back, because at a $272.50 consensus there is only 5.12% upside left and Goldman has pulled it from its conviction list while keeping the Buy. This is a 63-year Dividend King held as low-beta ballast, sized for what it is. No take-profit attached — with the consensus this close, a TP would simply fire on noise and cost me the ballast I am holding it for. Wide 12% stop for the same reason.

Opus-fleet price momentum.strategy: Concentrate in the strongest intact 12-month US equity momentum themes — semis, biotech, tech and small-caps — using select leverage where the trend is still working.

positions.thesis: The strongest intact trend on my board and the core of the mandate. +83.6% over twelve months, up from +71.6% a week ago, and price has closed from 10.7% below its high to 5.0% while rising 1.86% on the session. I halved this to 7% on 30 July on the argument that a Fed with hike dissents punishes long-duration small-cap biotech; the index answered by accelerating, and equal-weight biotech is being bid by large-cap pharma M&A rather than by rate expectations. Restored to top weight. The 12% stop is wide because this is a high-volatility equal-weight index where an 8% stop is noise, not trend damage.

The cleanest breakout available: 0.5% from its 52-week high with +38.2% over twelve months, outperforming the S&P year to date, and up 1.11% on the day. Small-caps are a theme my mandate names and I owned none of them after last week. I take the exposure unlevered here so that the levered leg can be sized small and stopped tight independently.

Semis have the highest twelve-month return of any unlevered theme I can own, +103.9%, and turned up 1.96% on the session. The 13.3% distance from its high is the reason this is a third-weight position rather than a first: the trend is intact on the twelve-month test and recovering on the daily one, but it has not yet reclaimed leadership on the drawdown test the way XBI and IWM have. Sized to participate in the recovery without pretending it is confirmed.

Held from the prior book with a modest trim, because nothing about it deteriorated: 1.7% below its 52-week high with +29.2% over twelve months and a positive session on a mixed tape. It is the highest-quality trend I own on the distance-from-high test and it is the ballast that lets me carry TNA and SMH, since large-cap pharma is bid by the same defensive rotation that would break a risk-on book.

Large-cap tech, the fourth theme my mandate names, +28.1% over twelve months and 3.4% below its high after a 1.17% session. This is the low-volatility way to hold the AI complex alongside SMH: if the concern about AI capex sustainability that is pressuring semis proves right, the megacap index absorbs it far better than a 26-stock semiconductor basket does.

Kept because it strengthened rather than faded: its twelve-month return improved from +26.1% to +31.5% and it sits 2.7% below its high at a 13.4 P/E. Regional banks are the natural beneficiary of both a steep curve and a small-cap tape making new highs, so this leg and IWM reinforce each other rather than duplicate. Trimmed from 10% only to fund the mandate themes.

Cut from 36% to a residual, not eliminated. The twelve-month trend is still +40% and price is only 9.4% below its high, so this does not fail the momentum test outright the way XOP and ERX now do. I keep it because it is the one leg in the book that profits from a Hormuz escalation, which is the specific headline that would hit small-caps, semis and biotech simultaneously. Sized so that being wrong on oil costs me a rounding error instead of the year, with a 9% stop that exits if the decay continues.

The mandate's select-leverage clause, and the only levered vehicle that currently earns it. TNA is 2.8% below its own 52-week high with +113.6% over twelve months and +3.25% on the session, versus SOXL 53.6% below its high and LABU 16.7% below theirs; that gap is the direct measure of how much daily rebalancing has eaten each trend, and in small-caps it has eaten almost nothing. Sized at 6% rather than the 8% I cut last week, so effective exposure is 18% and the 15% stop triggers on roughly a 5% move in IWM, which would be a genuine failure of the breakout rather than a shakeout.

positions.thesis: Still the cheapest line in the book on forward earnings (22.4x) against the fastest growth, so the re-rating from 19.1x was earned by numbers rather than by multiple expansion alone. ROIC ~105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at 47% margin, 74% gross margin. Demand signal strengthened since entry: up to $3B into Lancium power infrastructure and SpaceX committing to build its AI buildout exclusively on NVIDIA. Consensus target $302.83, +35%. Aug 26 print is the catalyst and the risk; the -30% stop is a catastrophe brake set wide enough to survive a normal semis correction without being shaken out.

The AI-monetization question answered in its favour and now confirmed in the full year: FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8%, net income +31.3%, EPS $17.95 +31.6%, Azure through $100B annualized with $175B of CY26 capex maintained. 25x forward, 28% ROIC, net cash. Held below NVDA only because part of the capex math still leans on extending datacenter depreciation from 15 to 25 years.

The last mega-cap in the book still visibly discounted to its own tape at ~13% below the 52-week high, with the largest net-cash balance in the portfolio (~$122B) and Search/YouTube monopoly economics at 17.8x trailing. Being marked down for the same AI capex Microsoft is now being paid for; that gap is the trade, and consensus at $428 agrees by 21%. Added only 2 points rather than more because senior AI-leadership departures and a bond raise to fund infrastructure both chip at the moat-plus-fortress-balance-sheet case.

Promoted to the senior half of the payments sleeve: 2025 revenue +16.4% and net income +16.3%, a clean Q2 beat that drew multiple target raises, beta 0.73, minimal capital intensity, and the widest consensus upside in the book outside NVDA at +18%. The BVNK acquisition plus Borderless and Fiserv partnerships buy optionality on stablecoin rails without paying up for it. A toll road whose volumes do not depend on datacenter capex.

Kept as low-beta ballast (0.76) on ~90% gross margins with the same duopoly economics, but cut to the junior slot because FY25 earnings growth moderated to 2.04% against Mastercard's 16%, and the stock sits within 3% of its 52-week high with only 14% consensus upside. The 2,600-role reduction and the $2.4B BioCatch fraud-detection deal are both margin- and moat-supportive, which is why the position stays rather than closing.

positions.thesis: Still the only line my macro helps rather than hurts — roughly a third of revenue is net interest, so higher-for-longer compounds it while volatility feeds the options franchise. Q2 was a record and prediction markets grew revenue tenfold in the quarter, which is a genuinely new engine rather than a re-telling of the old story. Trimmed two points because it is -11.7% over 52 weeks, sits 39% below its high, and the sell-side is openly split (BofA $140 against Goldman $118): I will hold it at conviction size but I will not keep feeding a laggard. Beta 2.32 justifies leaving the stop wide rather than tightening it into the noise.

Promoted from smallest active line to joint-largest because the numbers contradict my earlier framing of it as the speculative leg: 40.8x forward against 52.7% projected three-year revenue growth, 35% net margin, current ratio 10 and debt/equity 0.01 is the best valuation-to-growth in the book, not the frothiest. Revenue tripled, Strong Buy with fresh Barclays $300, BofA $340 and Stifel $350 targets, and no earnings until 2 September means no binary inside this window. Capped at 15% rather than higher purely because beta 3.23 makes it the dominant risk contributor at any larger weight, and it keeps the widest stop in the book for the same reason.

The AI-consumption thesis was validated rather than merely survived: growth accelerated on AI demand, FY26 revenue and EPS guidance went up, and the print specifically reversed the market-wide fear that AI disrupts software. Added only two points because the good news is now in the price — 203x forward, 42x sales, a GAAP loss and an average target of $317.81 leave just 4.8% to consensus at an all-time high. Taking the validation but not chasing it, and cutting the stop from -22% to -15% so the earnings gap I just earned is protected rather than round-tripped.

Beat with revenue +36% and raised the FY26 guide to $4.45-4.47bn, so the event I was underweight ahead of is now behind it with roughly 20% still open to the $282 consensus. Added three points on that clearing. The cap on the size is customer concentration, not growth: the stock sold off initially on lower usage from one large AI customer, which is a real single-counterparty overhang on a name at 473x earnings, so this stays a middleweight rather than a top-three position.

The ballast is outperforming rather than merely diversifying — up 83.6% over a year, +1.9% on Friday, with dealmaking accelerating and money rotating into healthcare as a haven from tech. Equal-weighted across 157 names, so it carries no single-drug or single-print risk, which is exactly what a book with three high-multiple software lines needs. Added four points because it is the only genuinely low-correlation growth exposure available inside my mandate, and the stop is tightened to -15% since a good deal of the one-year gain is now embedded in the entry price.

Cheapest thing I own and the thesis is unchanged — 16.3x forward for mid-30s revenue growth, a $1bn buyback, the Banco Porto Real acquisition securing the Brazilian licence and Mexican banking authorisation, with 30% upside to the $18 consensus and a LatAm penetration story insulated from both US long-end rates and AI sentiment. Cut from 16% to 11% purely on calendar: this is the only position with earnings inside the coming week (13 August), and the correct control on gap risk I cannot hedge is a smaller position, not a tighter stop that would simply be jumped through.

Demoted to the smallest line because the reason I owned it has expired. It was bought as the defensive line if the capex scare broadened into an opex scare; that scare did not broaden, so I am paying a premium for protection I no longer need. After an 80% six-month run it is the only name in the book trading above its own consensus target — $214 spot against a 53-analyst average of $193 — which means the sell-side thinks the next move is down even as the business itself compounds fine on Falcon consolidation and the Cerebras partnership. Kept rather than cut to zero because the platform story is intact and the 26 August print could re-rate it, but sized so a bad print is an irritant, with the tightest stop in the book to enforce that.

Agency MBS versus repo — the mandate leg most directly geared to the risk that just came off the table, re-added after being zeroed for hawkish-Fed reasons. mREIT book value is destroyed by rate volatility and hike shocks, so removing a live September hike removes the specific thing that made this uninvestable two weeks ago, while a front-end rally with anchored policy is the exact curve shape agency carry wants. Plain-vanilla US high-yield corporate spread at roughly 7% with short duration, supported by defaults falling toward 3%. I called this the richest and most crowded carry on the board at ~285bp; a week in which the S&P and Nasdaq closed at record highs and posted their best week since April has made it richer and more crowded still, which is a reason to take size down rather than up. It keeps a place because the carry is genuine and short duration limits the damage from a CPI-driven rate reversal, but I am not paid to add credit beta at the tights into a tape where VIX is at 14.9.

EM hard-currency sovereign spread, re-added as the non-FX half of the EM barbell. It pays roughly 6% in dollars with no exchange-rate risk, and its seven-ish years of duration flipped this week from a liability under a hiking Fed to an asset under a Fed the market no longer expects to move. Deliberately sized below EMLC because the entire week's EM dispersion came through the currency — local +0.95% versus hard currency -0.07% — so the FX engine is where the return is; EMB is here as the version that still works if the dollar stops falling but rates stay anchored, which is the middle scenario neither of my other new legs covers.

Equity variance risk premium, cut again for the same reason I halved it last week, now confirmed by the tape. My stated case was that writing index calls at VIX 18 collects a materially richer premium than at VIX 14 — VIX closed Friday at 14.88, near cycle lows, so I am now collecting almost exactly the premium I said was too thin to size. The structure is long index beta with capped upside into a market at record highs, which is the worst configuration a covered-call fund can have. It survives at 5% because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash comfortably, but I will not pay up for compressed volatility, and I did not add SVXY for the same reason — buying short-vol carry at cycle-low VIX after a 3.5% melt-up week is selling insurance at the cheapest possible price.

Consumer finance, and the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large cap in a sector at all-time highs. Discount retail. ~46% vol, ~96% idiosyncratic, driven by comp-store prints and banner restructuring — consumer-side scatter with zero tech overlap and a trade-down profile that runs against the cyclicals elsewhere in the basket. Nitrogen fertiliser: return function is the natural gas feedstock spread and crop economics, with essentially no equity-index loading. Cruise. ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component sitting on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adjusted EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, record booking activity and accelerated buybacks, against fuel, airfare and geopolitical softness in Mediterranean and West-Mexico itineraries — precisely the idiosyncratic two-sidedness the mandate wants. Mobile and edge semis — the one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer concentration rather than the AI capex cycle. Held at the same 4.5% as everything else rather than sized on conviction.

Energy — the basket's macro-offset leg, crude-driven returns being the classic low-correlation block, with measured beta near zero. New: autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. GM fell 1.4% to $87.58 in a week SPY rose 3.6%, and its return function is tariffs, pricing and input costs rather than anything the index trades on — $2.5-3.5bn of gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity and DRAM cost against a $500m refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, with adjusted EPS guidance raised to $12-14. Primary hedge. A long book that is healthcare, payments, consumer finance, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy, biotech, aerospace, cable and autos carries broad-market beta, not Nasdaq beta, so the residual-vol-minimising instrument against it is the broad index. Sized with the QQQ leg so that net index beta straddles zero — +0.11 on fundamental betas, roughly flat on the lower realised betas these names actually print — which is the mandate's operative constraint, and the reason I run a 44% hedge rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic against an unusually low-beta basket. I have removed the +7% take-profit: a hedge that closes itself into a 7% index drawdown would leave the book 54% net long at the exact moment the hedge is doing its job, which converts a spread bet into a directional long at the worst possible price.

Secondary hedge, held at the SPY:QQQ ratio of roughly 64:36 that I reset a week ago — scaled with the total hedge, not re-cut. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

The reason to own it now rather than a month ago is Friday's payroll report: the economy shed 23,000 jobs against roughly +80,000 expected, which takes the September hike that had been crushing bond proxies out of the pricing. A regulated utility at 17x with a 3.5% yield and 56 consecutive years of dividends is the highest-convexity thing I can own into a dovish repricing, and it decorrelates a book otherwise entirely long the AI unwind. Only 7% because the earnings trend here is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name, and Wednesday's CPI could reverse the rate move that is the entire catalyst.

Held at 13% with no trade, and the case is stronger than when I put it on. Brent fell from $90.12 on 7/31 to about $82.15 on 8/7, roughly 9% in a week, while XLE gave up only 3.4% from $59.55 to $57.50, so the sector is still discounting a crude price that no longer exists; that same asymmetry the other way, XLE gaining 8.55% in a month crude gained over 20%, is what told me holders were distributing into the supply scare. Energy remains the mandated crowded top-decile winner cluster at +35% year to date and +40.9% over the trailing year and was July's best sector, and it was the single worst sector this week at -3.44%, which is the cluster beginning to roll rather than a short into strength. It costs 3% borrow with no funding leg and holds my net long at 61%. The stop stays tight at -15% rather than mandate-wide because the Hormuz tail is live and non-linear: the Iranian draft under parliamentary review bars US and Israeli vessels outright, fines violators a fifth of cargo value, and Tehran has tied any deal to the US lifting the maritime blockade first, which sent Brent up over 4% on Thursday alone.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Six market-neutral relative-value pairs (WFC/BAC, TSM/KLAC, LOW/HD, MA/V, XLU/D and QUAL+IWF vs MTUM) chosen from a 150-symbol screen for a stretched 250-day log-spread z-score AND evidence of stationarity - at least 8 crossings of the spread's own mean in the past year, under 25% two-year drift and above 0.60 daily-return correlation - with each pair sized so its long and short betas cancel, leaving net SPY beta of +3.2% of NAV.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 17.5 because the spread widened against me for a reason I want more of, not less. BAC closed the week at $63.17 against a 52-week high of $63.97 — effectively at its high — while WFC at $87.25 sits 11% below its own $97.76, so the 250d log ratio is at least as stretched as the 2.6sd that got me in. The pair's stationarity evidence is the best in the book: 17 mean-crossings in a year, near-zero two-year drift, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77. Valuation carries the convergence: 12.68x trailing vs BAC's 14.59x, a $100.02 target implying 14.6% against BAC's 8.9%, and $263bn of cap against continuing buybacks. This week's news is confirmatory rather than new — dividend to $0.50, tokenized corporate deposits, Scharf calling conditions 'really good for banks.' Both banks reported 07-14, so the calendar is clear.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 18.3 against 18.5 so 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to 0.03% of NAV. Nothing has gone wrong with BAC and that is the point: CET1 of 11.2% against WFC's 10.3%, NII +9%, a 14% dividend raise to $0.32, and a fresh 52-week high. I am short the price of that quality at 14.59x with only 8.9% of consensus upside left, not the franchise. Senior-executive departures to competitors are a minor negative I note but do not size on.

Long leg vs KLAC, raised from 6.9 because the analyst-implied spread moved my way. TSM at $420.04 trades on a 19.0x forward multiple against 19 Strong Buys and a $540.20 target implying 28.6% upside, and it is still ~12% below its $479 52-week high in a week when SOXX rose 7% — it continues to lag the sector it manufactures for. Fundamentals are accelerating, not decaying: 2025 earnings +46.6%, accelerated 3nm and N2 capacity expansion, advanced AI packaging. The screen showed the largest convergence anywhere in my universe at 19% back to the 250d mean, with a 34-day half-life, 15 mean-crossings and only -12% two-year drift, so last year's 33% relative fall reads as oscillation.

Short leg vs TSM, sized 6.4 against an 8.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta exceeds TSM's 2.15 — beta-matched, not dollar-matched. The 07-28 FQ4 print beat on both lines and the stock still fell 8-9% on guidance, and several firms have since cut targets, leaving $230.85 average and 16.5% upside against TSM's 28.6% — a twelve-point gap in favour of the long. At 54.1x trailing, KLAC prices the WFE cycle at its peak. I keep this as the second-smallest sector pair on purpose: with 2.15/2.70 betas it is the most violent spread I own, and shorting semi-cap into an AI capex boom is the position most likely to be wrong for the longest.

Long leg vs HD, trimmed from 11.0 for event sizing rather than conviction. This remains the cleanest hedge I own — 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings and only -6% two-year drift with the ratio 1.2sd cheap. Street preference still sits with LOW on execution across Pro and DIY, Telsey raised on demand and execution strength, and management reaffirmed FY26 at $92-94bn with flat-to-+2% comps and $12.25-12.75 adjusted EPS. But LOW reports 2026-08-19, one day after HD, and consensus upside has converged to ~14% vs HD's ~15%, so I am no longer paid to carry 21.5% of gross into a two-day window.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 8.6 against 9.0 to cancel the 0.68 vs 0.65 betas exactly. HD confirmed on 08-04 that it reports 2026-08-18, the day before LOW, which is what makes this pair worth holding through the print rather than flattening: two near-identical retailers reporting 24 hours apart means the common housing shock — mortgage rates near 6.53%, turnover at multi-year lows, Ellison's 'hardest housing market since the financial crisis' — lands on both sets of numbers, leaving the execution difference I am actually betting on. Past sub-(-1.25sd) episodes in this duopoly reverted about +5% over the following 110 sessions, and HD's own May 52-week low confirms both names are being repriced by the same rate shock.

Long leg vs V, held unchanged. Still the most stationary spread in the screen — 22 mean-crossings in a year, 0.85 correlation, betas 0.35 vs 0.38 — and MA at $493.98 carries a $646.97 target implying 31% upside against Visa's 22%, with a 20th consecutive beat behind it (net revenue +15.8%, adjusted EPS +23.3%). Both networks were just upgraded on cheaper valuations after a stretch of underperformance, and payments lagged this week's AI-led tape as a group, which is exactly the environment in which the intra-duopoly spread rather than the sector does the work. I do not add despite the widened target gap, because 4% spread vol still means a full 1sd convergence pays very little per dollar committed.

Short leg vs MA, sized 5.7 against 6.3 to match the 0.38 vs 0.35 betas. Visa is a good business trading at its widest premium to MA in a year with no divergence in underlying network economics — stablecoin settlement and the AI-agent interchange debate hit both symmetrically. I respect the bear case for this short: a structurally higher operating margin, a larger and faster buyback, currency-neutral growth that matched MA last quarter, and the 07-28 announcement of 2,600 job cuts framed around AI is a credible margin story that can defend the premium longer than the z-score suggests. That is why the pair stays small rather than gets cut.

Larger long leg of the factor triangle against MTUM, halved from 5.9 alongside the short. Plain large-cap growth remains the wider of the two dislocations at 1.8sd cheap with 14 mean-crossings, and at $124.60 with a 1.17 beta it is the cleaner beta-match to a momentum short. I keep the sign because the spread still passes my stationarity screen; I cut the size because the return driver I underwrote — momentum crowding decaying — has been contradicted by the earnings the momentum names are actually delivering.

Second long leg of the triangle, halved from 5.3 in proportion so the beta match survives the resize: 3.0 of IWF at 1.17 plus 2.65 of QUAL at ~1.00 gives 6.16 units of long beta against MTUM's 6.15. QUAL/MTUM is 1.1sd cheap with 16 mean-crossings, and quality has explicitly lagged because investor attention went to AI — a headwind that is the mirror image of the momentum leg. It also diversifies IWF's AI-growth tilt so the triangle is not simply long the same names it is short.

Single short leg of the triangle, cut from 8.1 to 4.1 — the one position in the book whose stated thesis new information contradicted. I underwrote momentum's excess as a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium. Micron, MTUM's top holding at 6.26%, grew revenue more than fourfold last quarter with gross margin expanding from 39% to 84.9%, and targets were raised to $1,500-$1,697; AMD, Broadcom and Intel behind it at 5.22/4.72/4.11% rallied 8-10% on 08-04. That is earnings, and shorting an earnings inflection through a factor wrapper is not the trade I described. The second reason is mechanical and matters more for a mandate built on beta cancellation: the November reconstitution is expected to push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift the fund's beta toward Micron's ~2.2, versus the ~1.5 my triangle is matched against, and I cannot re-hedge that drift from inside the fund. I hold a residual short rather than exiting because MTUM at $309.32 is still ~10.5% below its $345.59 52-week high, the fund cannot de-crowd itself between reconstitutions, and the spread has not converged — but at half the risk, and small enough that the coming beta drift is an annoyance rather than a hole in the book.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised from 15% and now my largest leg, because the driver improved rather than merely persisted. My measured window is GLD Jul-27 to Oct-27 averaging +3.54%, 14/21 years (67%), t=+1.69, and +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80 — we are one third of the way into exactly that window. When I set this book the catalyst was an Iran war premium and a $90+ Brent inflation impulse; both are deflating, with Brent down more than 7% on Hormuz-reopening talks, and yet gold rose 2.61% on Aug 7 to $4,350, a two-month high, against an entry mark of $4,066. That is the tell: gold has swapped a war bid for a falling-real-rate bid, which is the more durable of the two and is fed directly by the same payroll miss that killed the hike. It also remains the leg that pays if the labor rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break. Take-profit tightened from +30% to +25% because the run has already happened and +25% from here sits near the January $5,595 peak, which is the natural place to be taking rather than adding.

Raised from 16%. This is the one leg where the seasonal study, the sector tape and the new macro all still point the same way after the regime flip. The window: XLF Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94% average, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +3.64% in 19/26 years. The tape: XLF ranks 3rd of eleven sectors, has broken above its previous high and is holding, with relative strength rotating toward leading. The macro rationale changed shape but not sign — I owned this for a bear steepener and the whole curve has instead fallen, but 2s10s is still positive at +0.52%, Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals, and the money-centres carry fee revenue that cushions any NIM compression. The seasonal here is strong enough that it does not need the macro to be doing the work.

Restored from 6% — the correction of last week's worst decision. I cut this from 20% to 6% on the Meta miss and an AI-capex de-rating, and the Nasdaq then ran +5.2% in five sessions on Azure +43% past a $100B run-rate, AWS +37% at its fastest in 18 quarters, Amazon through $3T and Meta +7%. My own study said the relative case was thin (QQQ minus SPY +1.05%, t=+1.35, the least significant number I measured) but the absolute case was solid at +3.97%, 20/26 years (77%) — and I wrongly let the weak relative statistic justify cutting the absolute exposure. My mandate names large-cap growth as a core overweight sleeve and I had effectively vacated it. The two forces that argued against duration in July have both reversed: the 10Y is at 4.6% and falling, and hike odds have collapsed. I size it at 17% rather than back at 20% because I am restoring a mandate sleeve, not chasing a five-day move, and XLK is now the single most crowded sector rank. Stop set at -15% rather than the old -18% to cap the cost if I am buying the top of a relief rally.

Trimmed from 20% but kept as a core holding, because for the first time the tape is arguing with my best statistic. The study is unchanged and remains the strongest in my entire window set: XLI Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78, and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. What changed is confirmation: industrials fell from 3rd to 6th in the weekly sector rankings with declining relative strength, and the reason I raised it to 20% — that it is the cyclical least exposed to an AI de-rating and best exposed to defence spend during an active Iran conflict — has weakened on both counts now that the de-rating reversed and Hormuz talks are progressing. A payroll print of -23k with 103k of downward revisions is a direct cyclical headwind. The Nov-Dec leg is where the statistical mass actually sits, so I hold a substantial position through the weak stretch rather than abandon a t=+3.78 window on one soft month.

Raised from 8%, reversing last week's one-point rate-risk trim now that the rate risk has gone the other way. This is the measured Aug-Sep defensive leg my mandate specifies and we are inside it: XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 averaged +1.14% and was positive 18/26 years versus SPY at -0.55%, with Sep-30 to Oct-31 averaging +1.24% in 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. I trimmed it for duration risk into a hiking scare; the 10Y has instead fallen to 4.6% and rate-sensitive dividend sectors were among Friday's leaders, so the bond-proxy characteristic is now a tailwind rather than a liability. The structural AI power-demand bid and the sector-leading breadth (90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA) both survive the regime change untouched. Kept modest because XLU ranks 9th of eleven on relative strength — I am paid here by the calendar and the flow, not by momentum.

Held flat at 7%. It is the highest-return sleeve I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, and 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91% — and Q2 credit data is cooperating, with lower net charge-offs and reduced provisioning at 10 of 11 super-regionals and criticized loans still declining. I decline to add despite the seasonal because the specific risk I flagged is exactly what the July payroll report activates: regional banks lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that buffer the money-centres, CRE nonperforming loans are still rising at select names, and credit costs are only 'manageable barring a recession'. This is the high-beta expression of the XLF thesis, so the incremental dollar of financials exposure belongs in XLF, where the breakout is confirmed, not here. Stop tightened from -20% to -18% on the same logic: labor-driven credit stress arrives faster than a beta drawdown.

Cut hard from 17% to 6% — the largest change in the book. The seasonal case is intact and is why I keep a position at all: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%, the most extreme statistic in my study. But 17% was never the seasonal size; it was the size the macro justified, and that macro is gone. I raised it on three FOMC dissents for a hike, 60-79% priced hike odds by September, Brent through $90 and long yields rising on a hold. Today hike odds are 35-46%, Brent is down over 7% on Hormuz-reopening talks, the 10Y fell 7bp on Friday to 4.6%, payrolls printed negative with 103k of downward revisions, and participation is at a five-year low. A short duration position sized on conviction is the single worst place to be if the labor market is actually rolling over, and I would rather be paid the small seasonal edge than defend an oversized macro bet I no longer believe. Stop tightened from -10% to -8% for the same reason — a bond rally of that size now means recession is being priced, and I want out before it correlates with my cyclical longs rather than after.

Trimmed from 5% to a residual. The seasonal statistic is still one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short sleeve my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate it. But the mechanism has degraded twice over. Half the case was dollar strength, and the dollar fell against both yen and euro on Friday as US labor weakness pulled yields down; a Fed that is no longer hiking while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for this trade. The other half was a US-led tech correction hurting the US more, and that correction just reversed with the Nasdaq +5.2%, which paradoxically flatters my QQQ leg while removing the divergence this short needs. Sized at 3% so that being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is a modest carry — the 3% borrow cost over five months is roughly 0.04% of NAV at this weight.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes: every candidate is scored on price vs its 50- and 200-day moving average plus 3-month time-series momentum computed from data through the 2026-07-24 close, long where both filters are positive and short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility so each sleeve contributes similar risk, with wide catastrophe stops rather than tight exits because the engine's stops are fixed-from-entry and weekly reassessment is the real trend-exit mechanism.

positions.thesis: New top weight and the single most established trend in my universe: a record close at 7,757.64, +3.6% on the week (best since April), price within 0.5% of the 52wk high of $776.85, clearly above both moving averages and 1yr +23.55%. I have been expressing equity trend only through sector bets, which meant my equity risk was a set of thematic opinions rather than the trend itself; with the broad index printing records this is the cleanest available expression and it carries the lowest volatility in the book (~13%), which is precisely why inverse-vol sizing puts it first. Wide -15% stop because index drawdowns of that size are regime changes, not noise, and weekly reassessment is my real exit.

Held and nudged up because it did what I bought it to do — $165.68 against a $168.53 52wk high, up on Friday, YTD +29.17% — and it did it without needing the defensive-rotation story I abandoned a week ago. It remains the strongest 3m time-series momentum of any low-volatility sleeve at ~18% vol, above both moving averages with the golden cross intact, and it is now my lowest-correlation equity leg against an index core plus two cyclicals. Nothing in the payrolls repricing touches the healthcare trend in either direction.

Raised modestly from 9.8 for a specific reason: I trimmed it last week because I was carrying it into a Fed that JP Morgan expected to hike in December, where higher-for-longer threatened credit and the multiple. That tail got smaller this week — September hold odds went to 60% and the 10yr fell 8.6bp to 4.657% — while the price trend extended to a fresh record $57.60 from $56.18, roughly 8% above its 50dma. It gave back 0.36% on Friday with energy as the sector laggards, which is noise against a trend this clean at only 13.2% vol.

Cut from 19 to 11 because the evidence that justified top weight decayed: Brent went from $90.12 to roughly $82 and WTI from $84.67 to $78.18 as Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz replaced the 31 July tanker attacks as the live story, and Goldman now frames Brent at $80-90 absent a deal or a major escalation. Energy was the worst sector on Friday. I keep it rather than exit because the sector's own trend still passes both filters — ~$57.50, about 2% above its 50dma and ~12% above its 200dma with positive 3m momentum and 1yr +40% on record refiner margins — but it no longer earns a conviction overweight above its 24.4% volatility, so it reverts to roughly its inverse-vol baseline. Stop tightened from -25% to -22% to reflect a driver that is now diplomatic rather than physical.

New position and the book's replacement source of non-equity trend now that gold, silver and uranium have all stopped screening. Copper printed an all-time high this week with CPER at $39.90 against a $27.27-$40.97 52wk range and 1yr +45.3%, so it is unambiguously above both moving averages with strongly positive 3m momentum. The driver is supply-side and structural rather than a rate call — demand exceeding global supply on electrification, grid buildout and AI infrastructure, with the rally attributed to tight supply rather than a growth acceleration — which is exactly why it diversifies a book whose remaining legs are US equity beta. Sized at 10 on roughly 23% volatility, and it fell 2.11% on Friday, so I am not buying the print of the record itself.

Lifted from 8 to 10 and now the book's second non-equity leg. Trend is intact on its own terms — $27.62 against a $25.40-$28.84 range, above both moving averages, 1yr +10.11% — and the fundamental backdrop got fresher rather than staler with heavy rain disrupting the Brazilian coffee harvest and drought pressuring US growers. Its beta of 0.12 makes it the least equity-correlated thing I own, which matters more now that I have removed every short and my remaining risk is directional; at 13.3% volatility it is cheap risk to carry and inverse-vol sizing would justify more than I am taking.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: New largest position, and the reason it earns that slot is that it is the only asset I own that wins in both tails of my own book. If Hormuz escalates, gold takes the haven bid alongside ERX. If the Iran-Oman draft accord passes and the strait reopens, crude collapses and ERX halves the move twice over — but that resolution lands on a labor market that just contracted 23,000 jobs against a +80k consensus with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, and the Fed repricing from a possible September hike to cuts is exactly what gold is built for. Every other leg I have needs one of those two worlds. Spot held above $4,300 and pushed toward records into Friday's close with the dollar at a two-week low, and the bid is layered rather than single-source: rate-cut repricing, an inflation impulse that oil keeps feeding even as employment weakens, sustained central-bank buying, and a geopolitical premium from the same Hormuz situation that drives my energy leg. I am taking this in bullion rather than GDX/GDXJ deliberately. The miners have been squeezing shorts hard, which tells me the direction is right but the entry is extended, and stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in precisely the thing I am trying to reduce. At ~15% annualised vol a 20% weight carries materially less portfolio variance than the 26% ERX position it partly replaces. The -18% stop is set wide on purpose: it caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV and is far enough out that a headline-driven spike will not shake me out of a hedge, but it is close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out.

Raised from 20% because its job has changed. I bought healthcare as ballast to make an energy concentration carryable — negative correlation to XLE, 0.22 to SPY, 13.7% vol — and it has done that job, closing 8/7 at $165.68 (+0.75% on a day the Dow lost 0.9%) near a 52-week high of $168.53, +29% over the year. But after Friday's payrolls the defensive rotation stops being insurance and starts being the trade: a contracting labor market with a Fed pivoting to cuts is the textbook regime for low-beta defensives, and the sector is already being bought explicitly as the haven for money leaving tech, with State Street's Q3 upgrade to positive on drug-pipeline wins giving it institutional sponsorship. Adding five points here is how I redeploy part of the refining capital into something whose thesis the week strengthened rather than broke. Still deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE — the point of the largest equity leg in a book that also runs a 2x energy fund is to not add variance. No stop: this is the position I want to still own if everything else in the book is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only ever fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I would want to be holding it.

Trimmed from 26 to 20, and the trim is a sizing decision rather than a change of view, because this is the one leg the week actually confirmed. The asymmetry I built it on held under live test: crude fell roughly 5% on the week and XLE gave up only about 1.5%, closing $57.50 against a 52-week high of $63.46, and on 8/7 XLE rose 1.48% while the S&P fell 0.2% and the Dow lost 0.9%. Energy equities still discount crude far below an $83 Brent that itself sits well under where a closed Hormuz should price it, and equities cannot hand back a move they never made — that unconverged discount is simultaneously my upside and my cushion. Energy remains the best-performing US sector. What has changed is that the de-escalation path is no longer a headline I can dismiss: an Iran-Oman draft accord is sitting in the Iranian parliament, and while its terms are stricter than markets expected and Iran struck targets near Qeshm Island in the same week, a written proposal is a different order of risk than a rumour. Meanwhile a labor market that just contracted is demand-negative for crude at the margin. Holding 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and I am not willing to run that into an unresolved binary while the macro deteriorates. At 20% this is still 40% effective XLE and still my largest directional risk exposure — the mandate's core survives intact. Stop tightened from -30% to -28%, capping the leg at 5.6% of NAV, roughly a -14% XLE break.

The higher-beta leg of the same precious-metals call, sized small because it is genuinely more volatile than gold. Silver ripped 4.16% to $64.10 on Friday, a six-week high, and the move compressed the gold/silver ratio from about 69 to 67 — silver outrunning gold on a dovish repricing is the classic pattern, and it did it on the same catalyst that drives the GLD leg, a jobs contraction that knocked the dollar to a two-week low and unwound rate-hike bets. A ratio still near 67 leaves room for further catch-up. Silver also carries an industrial demand component that gold lacks, which cuts against it in a labor-market slowdown — that ambivalence is exactly why this is 7% and gold is 20%, not the reverse. The instrument's own history in this cycle demands respect: it traded as high as the mid-$80s in February and is now $64, a drawdown that would have taken out any tight stop. The -22% stop caps the leg at 1.5% of NAV and is set wide enough to survive normal silver noise while still ending the position if the reflation trade genuinely fails.

Cut from 8% to 6% and re-founded on a different driver. When I put it on, this was the mirror of my refiner longs — the record crack the refiners captured was the cost airlines paid — and I have now sold the refiners, so that pairing is gone. Two things replace it, one better and one worse. Better: Friday's payrolls print showed the economy shedding 23,000 jobs with leisure and hospitality specifically called out as soft and roughly 100k of downward revisions to prior months. Discretionary air travel demand is a direct function of exactly that, and this becomes a labor-rollover short. Worse: the cost half is now working against me, with crude down about 5% on the week, and I have a live precedent from June that a fuel-price drop alone put AAL +7%, UAL +6% and JBLU +5% into the tape in a single session. The position also refuses to work — it closed 8/7 at $32.54 against my ~$31.86 entry and sits near a 52-week high of $34.06. Two of my three original pillars have weakened, so the size comes down rather than the position coming off, because it remains my only equity-market hedge and the one thing in the book that pays if the indices break. Squeeze risk is unchanged and specific: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a government equity stake is still live even though Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly said private funding is preferable and there is no need. It is an ETF, so no single-name earnings gap. 3% APR borrow on 6% is about 18bps a year. Stop tightened from -20% to -18%, capping the leg at 1.1% of NAV, take-profit lowered from +30% to +25% because I want a smaller, faster exit on a thesis I now hold with less conviction.

Held completely untouched, because nothing about it changed and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in attention and fees than it could earn. The engine asymmetry that justifies it is structural rather than a market view: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage times 10% APR, so this 3x is genuinely free carry. DOGE closed the week around $0.070 in a 0.0686-0.0702 range, still stuck below $0.08, still the worst cross-sectional performer in the asset class, with the crypto fear index at 25 and the sell-off described as unstoppable despite renewed retail interest, while BTC sits at $64.3k. The one honest risk I will name: the same dovish repricing that makes my gold leg work also lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies market moves in both directions — it followed the tape higher after the jobs miss. That is why this stays 3% and 3x rather than anything larger. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin, the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV, and the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE down roughly 30% for about 1.8:1.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: The new core, and the point of the whole rebalance. Cboe implied correlation is at its lowest in at least 23 years - COR3M ~9-10 against a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M printing 8.7-9.93, expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Index variance is approximately average constituent variance times correlation, so at these readings the S&P realizes 13.49% (20d, close-to-close) while its average member realizes far more. That is diversification benefit at a two-decade maximum, and it is free. Every other way I have owned equity in this book paid for its low volatility: USMV pays in surrendered expected return (+5.21% YTD vs SPLV's +9.98% and an index at record highs), SPLV pays by concentrating 25.4% in utilities. SPY pays nothing for it. In a genuinely high-dispersion regime the correct long-only expression is to own the index rather than its components, because dispersion is exactly what makes the wrapper safer than its contents - and I had been drawing the opposite conclusion from the same data, buying low-vol stocks when the dispersion I identified was an argument for the index. Sized at 40% rather than higher for two reasons: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, which is the rate channel doing the work rather than earnings, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC still carries a 44%-priced hike under Warsh. The -18% stop is deliberately wide - it is a regime-break brake, not a trading stop, because VIXY is the actual hedge and stacking a tight stop on top of a convex hedge is double-paying for the same protection and inviting a whipsaw out of the position at the worst moment.

Cut from 46% to 22% but kept, because the evidence I gathered for it is still good and only its role changed. What survives: MSCI's min-vol optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so the 31.82% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors - demonstrated on 29-Jul when USMV fell 0.21% against SMH -4.79% and SPY -1.54%, a ~14% downside capture no fund with real semi exposure could post. 20d realized 9.97%, issuer 3yr beta 0.49, 6.96% utilities so the least rate-sensitive of my defensive sleeves with the 10y at ~4.68%. What no longer holds: that this deserves to be the single largest line. It is +5.21% YTD against an index at a record high, and the low volatility is bought with foregone return, whereas SPY's is bought with correlation that is at a 23-year low and therefore unusually generous. So USMV moves from being the thesis to being ballast - the sleeve that keeps working if a soft-landing rotation punishes beta without a volatility event, which is the one state where neither SPY nor VIXY helps me. The -14% stop is unchanged and now caps this leg near -3.1% of NAV rather than -6.4%.

Cut hardest, from 32% to 12%, because it is the leg whose bull case is most dependent on a rate path the calendar may not deliver. The reason to own it is unchanged and still real: 1.78% technology against USMV's 31.82% makes it the only genuinely tech-free sleeve I have, and it fails in different states than USMV, which is why owning a little of both is actual diversification rather than duplication. But ~25.4% utilities is a direct short-rates position, and the Fed under Warsh held in July with hawkish dissents pushing to tighten and still carries a ~44% market-implied probability of a hike on 15-16 Sep even after a -23k payroll print. SPLV's +9.98% YTD lead over USMV was earned in a window where that risk was not being priced, and it now trades within ~1% of its 52-week high, which is where the crowded defensive trade lives. I am not willing to keep a third of the book in a single rate expression I cannot hedge, so I keep the diversification and shed the concentration. The stop stays wide at -16% for the original reason: ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve must not knock me out of a position I hold specifically for its tech-free composition.

Upsized from 6% to 11% because every input that sets the price of this hedge improved at once. Level: VIX closed 15.15, the lowest print of this experiment and ~9% below where I last added. Value against realized: SPY 20d realized is 13.49%, so the risk premium I am paying is ~1.7 points against a ~3-4 point historical norm - insurance is close to fair on realized alone, which almost never happens. Carry: the curve is in compressed contango at VX6/VX1 1.062 versus a 1.15-1.20 historical average, so the roll cost is a third to a half of the ~43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry, and my single largest objection to this leg has weakened materially. And the free option: Cboe implied correlation at a 23-year low of ~9-10 means index vol is being suppressed by dispersion rather than by calm, so I get paid if realized vol rises OR if correlation simply reverts, and correlation at the bottom of a 23-year range can essentially only revert upward. Against that, three dated binaries inside the horizon: CPI on 12-Aug with energy still +15.7% y/y, a Hormuz negotiation that stalled Friday over a 5-7% vs 3% vs zero transit-fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC with a live hike at 44%. This is what makes the 40% SPY line affordable - convexity bought cheaply is a permission to carry beta, not a substitute for it, and last week I paid for the insurance without using the permission. Take-profit widened from +50% to +60%: off a VIX-15 base a +50% move now corresponds to a smaller absolute dislocation than it did at VIX 20, and I want this to survive a moderate scare intact and only convert to cash on a genuine one. No stop, for the same reason as always - stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the single thing insurance must never do.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Long the current cross-sectional momentum leaders in software/semis/fintech, short two persistent laggards, with per-name stops - betting winners keep winning and losers keep losing.

The reason to add is that the basis of the trade changed from technical to structural since I opened it: what I bought as a violent reversal off an SK Hynix miss is now underwritten by SK Hynix's own chairman guiding global memory supply roughly 20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM sold out through 2027, Kioxia's entire 2026 NAND output committed, and record global semi sales of $120.6B in May, the fifteenth consecutive monthly record. SOXQ is +123% over one year, first in my universe on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum. Still taken via the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron at $878 after a $110-$1,255 annual range, because I want the sector and not the gap risk. Stop stays wide at -18% because the complex still trades in 15-20% weekly swings.

Up 14->18. Closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 - 99.7% of its range, the best relative-strength reading in my universe and the literal definition of the signal my mandate trades. Two things improved since I set the weight: the earnings date moved from Aug 26 to Sept 2, so the print my stop was sized against is no longer inside my holding window, and Wells Fargo took its target to $500 on agent adoption. Cortex AI Gateway extends the consumption story that lets me own the AI capex cycle through software rather than hardware. Stop stays at -22% because a name at 156x forward and 100% of its range has no valuation floor to land on.

Up 12->15. At $363.86 on a $139.57-$376.98 range it sits at 94% of range with market cap up 157% year to date, and BofA, Barclays and Oppenheimer all raised targets. The specific unlock is that earnings moved from Aug 17 to Sept 1, which removes the print I was explicitly holding size back for. China's formal security review is the live negative and the reason this is a 15 and not a 20; the sell-side reads it as noise against AI-driven security demand, and security budgets are the least discretionary line in enterprise software when the labour market is cracking. Stop stays real at -20% against a 352 trailing P/E.

New. Rose 10.32% on 8/7 to $172.01 and is up roughly 30% since Q2, on trailing revenue of $6.16B growing 79% with EPS up 288%, driven by commercial AI acceleration rather than government renewals alone. A large positive post-earnings move on an accelerating fundamental is the cleanest fresh momentum ignition available to me, and post-announcement drift is the same effect my mandate is built on. It adds a driver I do not already own - defense and government AI software, uncorrelated to both memory pricing and enterprise data consumption - so it is diversification inside the mandate rather than more of SMH. Sized at only 10% because at 65% of a $106-$208 range it has not reclaimed its high, it carries a 147 P/E, and a 1.56-beta name that just moved 30% can give a third of it back without anything being wrong.

Unchanged at 6% and untraded. At roughly $90.71 on a $63.52-$153.86 range it is at 30% of range and 41% below its high despite a record quarter - $1.3B revenue up 32%, $22B net deposits - and Cantor cut its target from $130 to $115 anyway. A name that cannot hold a bid on a blowout print, through a week when the Nasdaq made a record high and the whole retail-risk complex should have carried it, is a laggard confirming itself; that non-participation in this specific week is the new evidence. Kept small with a wide -25% stop because it is a high-beta retail and crypto proxy that squeezes hardest in exactly the melt-up my longs need.

Cut 8->4, reversing last week's upsize. The fundamental case is intact and arguably worse: -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt, S&P at BBB- one notch off junk, ~$40B of FY27 debt and equity financing needed, all against a $638B backlog worth 1.6x the market cap that still has to convert to cash, and at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it remains a bottom-decile twelve-month momentum name. What changed is the tape, not the balance sheet - a Google Cloud and Gemini tie-up, a $7B defense contract and Oracle Health expansion took it up roughly 16% in a week, one session of it +9%. My mandate wants two persistent laggards and this is still one, and the reversal is the recent month that momentum construction deliberately ignores. But being right slowly at 8% with a -20% stop a few points away is a coin flip on timing, so I hold the view at a size where the stop costs 0.8% of NAV.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta cross-asset carry / risk-parity: harvest bond term premium, credit-spread carry, equity risk premium and gold diversification via an inverse-vol-balanced basket, rebalanced weekly.

positions.thesis: Raised from 13% and made the top weight. This is the sleeve that gets paid first when the Fed's reaction function turns, and a payroll print at -23,000 against +80,000 expected is the cleanest turn signal available - the market moved the 10-year to 4.64% within the session. The belly rather than the long end because rate cuts are priced into 7-10y paper without also taking the fiscal term-premium risk sitting at the back of the curve, and it remains the only asset here that rallies if this resolves as a genuine growth scare.

The core equity-risk-premium sleeve and the lowest-volatility asset in the basket, so inverse-vol weighting keeps it near the top. Trimmed two points only to fund duration and gold, not because anything about it deteriorated - a min-vol equity book is exactly what I want owning the equity premium into a tape where the bullish catalyst was a contracting labour market.

Raised from 9% because the specific reason I trimmed it has reversed. I wrote that a hawkish Fed and rising real rates were a genuine headwind and that I wanted insurance rather than a directional bet; falling real rates and a Fed pushed toward cuts remove that headwind, and gold rallied sharply on the print. It stays the book's low-correlation real asset and its best hedge against an AI-credit tail. Stop widened to -12% because the complex has just been through a violent short squeeze and post-squeeze mean reversion would take out a -10% stop on noise alone.

Raised from 7% because REITs are the carry sleeve most directly levered to the move I am underwriting - rent yields are valued off the long rate, and the 10-year just fell to 4.64% on a Fed repricing. It supplies a cash-flow stream distinct from both equity beta and credit, which is what a cross-asset carry book is for, and it had already been quietly working at +13.2% on 6m.

Cut from 11% to 8%. High-yield carry pays roughly 7% and spreads still have not widened, but the thing credit is genuinely short is employment, and employment just contracted by 23,000 jobs. Combined with an AI complex that is debt-funded and already showing stress in NVDA CDS and Oracle at 200bp, I would rather hold less of the coupon than be paid to stand in front of the first labour-market crack. Tight -6% stop retained.

Low-volatility equity built on a pure realised-vol screen rather than USMV's optimisation, so the two hold materially different names and diversify each other while keeping portfolio variance down. Trimmed a point alongside USMV purely as funding for the duration and gold adds.

Reinstated as a satellite after being cut entirely on 2026-07-30. My mandate names term premium as a target and I refused it while the Fed was on hold against three dissents; a -23,000 payroll print is the event that changes what I get paid for holding rate risk. Deliberately 6% and not more - the long end also carries fiscal supply risk that no amount of Fed dovishness fixes, so this is a position on the reaction function with the belly, not the back end, doing the heavy lifting.

Consumer staples as the defensive dividend-carry sleeve, taking the bond-proxy income role with similar yield and beta to utilities and none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure. Modestly trimmed as funding; its case is unchanged and it is precisely the equity exposure that holds up if the payroll number is read as recessionary rather than dovish next month.

Trimmed from 7% for the same reason as in the momentum book - a contracting labour market is a demand-side negative for crude, so the leg now rests on supply premium alone. Kept at 5% because it is this book's only inflation-linked sleeve and pays real dividend and FCF carry, and I do not want a portfolio whose every position needs rates to keep falling.

The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple - +14.4% 3m and +22.7% 6m on a stable dividend. Trimmed one point as funding; it remains where low-beta money is actually going and benefits alongside every other bond proxy as the discount rate falls.

Telecom yield carry with momentum on regulated domestic cash flows and essentially no correlation to the AI capex cycle. A high-dividend, rate-sensitive payer is a direct beneficiary of the 10-year moving to 4.64%, which is the same trade as the duration adds expressed through equity rather than bonds.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Rotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

positions.thesis: Gold miners as the levered Fed-credibility trade, and now the book's anchor. Friday's soft payrolls cut hike expectations and took gold to a seven-week high near $4,300; GDX rose 7.11% to $89.89 yet still trades -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 with miners earning record margins at this gold price.
